doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Reissues, Artie Shaw and learning to produce from Monk
summary: He describes reissue work, a difficult session with Artie Shaw, his appreciation-and-facilitation view, and Monk as his first major artist.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: with doing this. The only real serious variation is that I have — I used to say in recent years — but for a lot of years, a lot of my attention has been focused on reissues and obviously the procedures are a little different there. For the most part that makes it possible to get into cliches like well I spent the whole day in the studio with Louis Armstrong or Duke Ellington or Fats Waller, and he didn’t give me a hard time. But that joke got busted about a year ago because one of my most recent reissue projects was with Artie Shaw, who is now 92, is quite firmly there, could not possibly have ever been more opinionated in his life than he is now, and so I could not say I spent the day with Artie Shaw and he did not give me a hard time. He did give me a hard time. But it was a wonderful experience working with him actually, and it literally I think it’s about the only circumstances under which you can be working on pre-tape material with the artist. And there ain’t too many people who still have firm opinions, he still doesn’t like “Begin the Beguine,” which after all I guess was a 1937 or 8 recording. Maybe it was ’36. I don’t have to remember those things, they’re all firmly written down. Those discographies are unchanging. But what I consider the most important work has been the things that I’ve been able to do with a very large handful of artists who are important, whose work is and should be lasting and you know I know for a minute that it’s not my creativity. My job was to do two things. One is to appreciate and the other is to facilitate. And I usually don’t use such glorious words to describe it but I’ve always been the guy that was able to get it done, which kind of surprises me sometimes. I don’t think of myself as being firm, as being decision-maker, I certainly do not believe in the auteur theory of jazz direction, I don’t think, and there have been people and we won’t bother to name names but there have been other jazz record producers who clearly do think of themselves as king makers. And I never did. It just got to be the point of hey, somebody’s got to make the decision and okay, that’s one of the things that I’m here for. Sometimes you might make decisions because nobody else is even in the position to even be aware of the need for a decision. Initially I learned I guess — well let me say this — everything I learned initially I learned from the best possible teacher as far as I’m concerned. I owe my entire career, whatever success I may have, the man that is firmly responsible for that is Thelonious Monk. There is no question in my mind that I gained tremendously from the initially very frightening fact that this was the first artist of any significance who I worked with. I mean I had done a few things — before I got involved with Thelonious I had been in the studio with people like Randy Weston, Mundell Lowe, Billy Taylor, you know all pussycats. But here was a real tough cookie. Here was a man who knew what he wanted, thought he knew exactly how to get it, frequently was right, and the example I used to use, in other words the old fashion way of teaching a child to swim is you toss him into the deep end of the pool and if he doesn’t go under he’s learned to swim. Well I learned — that’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
